>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
Flights are resuming across the United States following a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says problems with radar
and communications prompted the FAA to halt departures.
>> Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data.
They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers.
And because of that, we shut the system down.
>> Flights are moving again, but thousands of passengers remain stranded
as airlines work to clear the backlog.
Karen Phillips was at Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport in Atlanta
where her flight was delayed twice.
>> I mean, it's frustrating, but what can I do?
I can't get upset about something I can't control.
I'd rather be safe than, you know, catching a fit, but things happen.
>> On the West Coast, airports are also working to get flights back on schedule.
Steve Futterman is at Los Angeles International Airport.
>> At 2.30 this morning, there were already long lines here at LAX,
people hoping to get to all sorts of destinations.
This is the fifth busiest airport in the nation.
The ground stop left many people stranded, including Gary Mays.
He's trying to get back to Ohio.
>> I'm not sure, hopefully we get home today.
>> And just your reaction to having to deal with something like this?
>> Just be patient, just be patient, that's what you have to do.
I've traveled a lot in my life at times like this.
That's all you could do is be patient.
>> Many people without accommodations tried to turn their luggage
and luggage carts into makeshift beds.
Officials say it could take several days before everything gets back to normal.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Futterman at Los Angeles International Airport.
Flight aware lists more than 3,500 cancellations today for flights
within, into, or out of the U.S.
Some Republican state officials are trying to revive the Trump administration's push
for mail-in voting restrictions in time for the 2028 election.
NPR's Hansi Lo Wang reports a federal judge has blocked the U.S. Postal Service
from working on those restrictions for now.
>> More than a week after voting ended for this year's midterms,
Missouri State Attorney General is leading 11 other Republican state officials
in this push to shape the next federal election in 2028.
The U.S. Postal Service issued a revised mail-in ballot rule in August
in response to an executive order by President Trump.
Under that rule, USPS would refuse to deliver mail-in ballots to voters in states
where election officials do not turn over their voter lists to the mailing agency.
The Supreme Court blocked the USPS rule for the midterms.
Now these Republican state officials are appealing a lower court order
that's blocking USPS from working on the rule for the 2028 election.
U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols issued that order after finding
that the Postal Service likely has no authority
to impose these requirements on states.
The Trump administration is not appealing the order.
Hansi Lo Wang, NPR News.
>> This is NPR News.
Investigators are working to determine why a tanker struck a docked cruise boat
in New Orleans yesterday.
Mayor Helena Moreno describes how the evacuation turned into a rescue.
>> The passengers began disembarking from the ship after that collision.
But while that was happening, the cruise ship began to sink.
And then eventually, the cruise ship toppled over.
>> More than 30 people were taken to hospitals to be treated for injuries.
The National Transportation Safety Board says it's planning to investigate.
The Trump administration says it's allowing states to pause cutting people
from Medicaid if they aren't working.
NPR's Selena Simmons-Duffin reports the work requirements were a key part
of the Republican budget bill passed last year.
>> Medicaid work rules all around the country take effect on January 1st.
For months, Democratic state officials and advocates have warned
that the timeline was way too fast and that eligible low-income people could
lose health coverage by mistake.
Now the Trump administration has responded.
In a letter to state officials, it says states will have the option
to keep people enrolled even if they don't meet the work requirements for six months.
For states that opt in, no one will lose their Medicaid
because they aren't working until next summer.
There are several legal challenges that could still change the policy or its timeline.
And when Democrats take over the majority in Congress,
they'll try to reverse the policy altogether.
Selena Simmons-Duffin, NPR News, Washington.
